title: What Does Beijing Mean By ‘Strategic Stability’?
gist: Tsinghua scholar Sun Chenghao explains Beijing's 'strategic stability' framework agreed at the May Beijing and September Washington Trump-Xi summits as managed competition. He argues it should insulate the relationship from spillovers via regular summits, economic boards, military channels, AI risk dialogue and exchanges.

insights.claim: Trump and Xi agreed in May in Beijing to build a 'constructive relationship of strategic stability' and reaffirmed it in September in Washington, grounded in respect, fairness and reciprocity; it is framed as managed competition, not an end to competition.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: The stated frame for US-China relations is managed competition with a political floor.

insights.claim: Stability is meant to bound competition, covering how it is conducted, what ends it serves and how far it spreads, so that security measures do not turn every economic and technology interaction into a national-security battlefield.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: Implies Beijing seeks to ring-fence economic and tech ties from security disputes.

insights.claim: Strategic stability should be a floor under competition, not a ceiling on cooperation.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: A reusable test for whether bilateral gestures are stabilizing.
insights.quote: Strategic stability should provide a floor under competition, not a ceiling on cooperation.

insights.claim: Past US-China summit gains proved fragile: the December 2018 Buenos Aires trade truce was followed by tariff escalation in May 2019, and the November 2022 Bali meeting was followed by the February 2023 balloon incident that derailed Blinken's Beijing visit.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: Base rate: one-off summit truces have decayed within months, so discount single-meeting optimism.

insights.claim: Regular leader-level engagement could turn crisis management into strategic management, giving officials political space to fix problems before they become emergencies.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: A regular summit cadence would lower tail risk of abrupt trade or security ruptures.

insights.claim: If competition accelerates while management mechanisms stay weak, the present calm may prove to be only an intermission.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: Treat the current US-China thaw as reversible.

insights.claim: The main danger in US-China relations is cross-domain contamination: an export-control dispute can spill into security dialogue, a military encounter can freeze economic communication, and a cyber or AI incident can be read as strategic hostility.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: Event risk in one domain (chips, military, cyber) can hit others; hedge across them.

insights.claim: Economic mechanisms such as the Board of Trade and Board of Investment should keep functioning even when negotiations are difficult, and military channels should stay open when political relations worsen.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: Watch whether these bodies keep meeting during disputes as a stability indicator.
insights.locator: 'Economic mechanisms such as the Board of Trade'

insights.claim: On AI, the two countries need no grand bargain to discuss shared terminology, major safety incidents, cyber risks and human decision-making in high-consequence systems, and recent US-China economic talks have begun to include AI risks alongside trade.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: AI risk dialogue is becoming part of the formal trade agenda.
insights.locator: 'On AI, the two countries do not need'

insights.claim: At the Washington summit Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to China for study and exchanges over five years, aimed at the loss of firsthand mutual knowledge.
insights.speaker: Sun Chenghao
insights.so_what: A soft-power initiative whose follow-through is a gauge of sincerity.
